A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same internal-bias and overthinking study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison despite retitling, reorganization, and substantive experimental additions.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, attention analyses, answer-probability analyses, and MASK intervention results in Sections 4–5 and the appendices.

after.justification: v3 reports original model evaluations and question-removal results, alongside new bias-injection experiments and mitigation-method evaluations in Sections 4–7 and the appendices.

M1.justification: v3 adds a distinct bias-injection procedure: sample-specific LoRA fine-tuning on 50 declarative paraphrases before retesting the same question (Section 5.2, Appendix H). This substantially extends the intervention methodology. v1's MASK intervention matches the later question-removal intervention in purpose and timing.

E1.justification: The evaluation coverage remains bilingual CharCount, KnowLogic, AIME 2024, and AIME 2025; the AIME benchmarks exchange main-text and appendix placement. v3 additionally uses DeepScaleR as mathematical training data for the FCS-SFT experiment (Appendix I.1).

E2.justification: v1 compares MASK with original generation but does not evaluate competing mitigation methods. v3 Table 4 adds FCS-SFT, FCS-DPO, SEAL, and PROBE on CharCount, plus FCS-SFT on AIME 2024. Table 3 also introduces random-statement training controls for bias injection.

E3.justification: Appendix B changes direct-answer collection from one sample per template at four temperatures to 16 samples per template at temperature 0.5. v3 also introduces controlled training on high/low-bias subsets, FCS training datasets and budgets, and SEAL/PROBE calibration procedures (Appendices H–I), substantially expanding the experimental design.

E4.justification: v3 adds controlled correct/wrong bias-injection tests, PROBE threshold sensitivity analysis (Appendix F.3), and a layer-wise attention-ratio analysis (Figure 4b). Conversely, v1's Section 5.2.3 and Figure 5 probability-trace analysis, including its strongly biased subset, are removed rather than relocated.

E5.justification: Bias-distribution estimation now uses 64 sampled direct answers per question instead of 16 (Appendix B). Output-length standard deviations and attention error bars already existed in v1 and remain in v3. Additional standard-deviation tables extend that reporting practice; no confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-training seed information are added.

E6.justification: v3 adds bias-injection and mitigation results and revises existing values. QwQ-32B's KnowLogic low/high lengths change from 4526.4/5526.6 to 5694.7/7167.1 (Table 1). CharCount(zh) original/intervention accuracies change from 71.1%/69.4% to 73.4%/72.9% (Table 2). These are revised reported results, not established same-setting gains given the changed sampling and incomplete setting reconciliation. v1's probability-trace results are removed.

T1.justification: No new theoretical result, proof, or substantive mathematical revision is introduced. v3's bias-distance notation and normalized-attention equations formalize measurements already described in v1, while the reasoning-reduction ratio retains its meaning.

C1.justification: The central internal-bias explanation remains. However, the abstract, contributions, and conclusion shift from presenting MASK as a mitigation contribution toward two causal interventions and a new headline claim that tested mitigation methods leave internal bias influential. v3 also explicitly describes the reported length reductions as reductions in redundant reasoning.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the new trials as showing that shorter reasoning can coexist with persistent bias and that mitigation can impair complex-task accuracy. It adds a layer-specific bias-reactivation interpretation. It removes v1's explicit limitations concerning open-ended tasks, the unexplained origin of excessive attention, and reliance on manual decoding intervention.

D1.justification: Appendices H–I add training-data construction, LoRA and optimization settings, and SEAL/PROBE implementation details. Appendix B newly documents numerical outlier filtering. Conversely, v3 omits v1's explicit greedy-decoding and 100-example attention-sample disclosures. One new setting remains inconsistent: PROBE uses 0.9 in Appendix F.3's prose but 0.80 in Table 7.

R1.justification: The related-work sections retain their emphasis on explaining overthinking rather than merely controlling its behavior. v3 adds supporting references for dynamic early exit, LoRA, DeepScaleR, and layer interpretation, while making the relationship to previously cited mitigation approaches more concrete through experiments.

P1.justification: Beyond adding experiments, v3 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, conclusion, and measurement/attention exposition. It places causal interventions before a separate interpretability section, adds a mitigation section, replaces MASK terminology with question removal, and reorganizes the appendices. The title and author list also change.

P2.justification: v3 adds comparison, sensitivity, and standard-deviation tables; removes v1 Figure 5; expands Figure 4 with a layer-wise curve; and redraws attention charts with category colors and hatching. Figures and tables are extensively rearranged under a different document template. The existing AIME tables and most correlation plots are matched across relocation and renumbering.

improvement.justification: Controlled bias injection with random-statement controls (Table 3), implemented mitigation comparisons (Table 4), and detailed training instructions strengthen the empirical support and reproducibility beyond v1. The gain is tempered by removal of the probability-trace diagnostic and explicit applicability limitations, missing decoding details, and inconsistent PROBE threshold reporting. These tradeoffs support a useful but limited net improvement rather than treating the larger experimental scope as sufficient evidence of a substantial quality gain.
